newsitem.title: POLAND: Pope bids difficult farewell to Poland.
newsitem.headline: Pope bids difficult farewell to Poland.

text.p: Pope John Paul said farewell to his beloved homeland on Tuesday, telling Poles he was carrying the whole country in his heart and urging them to use their post-communist freedom wisely.

"Moments of farewell are always difficult," he said at a departure ceremony at Krakow airport at the end of an 11-day sentimental journey he used to prod Poles to exercise their new economic and political freedom in line with Christian values.

"I take my leave of you, beloved countrymen, with a profound awareness that this does not signify a breaking of the bond which unites me with you, which unites me with my beloved native land," he said before he was due to fly to Rome.
"As I return to the Vatican, I carry in my heart all of you, your joys and your cares, I carry my whole native land," the Pope said.
Earlier, at a lunch with bishops in the town of Krosno, the Pope said he felt capable of making another visit to Poland and would give serious attention to the possibility.
"Throughout this pilgrimage I have seen with optimism that I am capable of a new visit if God permits it," the Pope said.
Vatican officials have insisted that the trip was not planned to be the Pope's last to Poland.

Still, his 77 years and recent health problems made the journey more poignant as he travelled through the areas where he survived the horrors of World War Two, discovered his vocation and lived as priest, bishop and cardinal.

While his seventh trip home was filled with personal memories, it also gave him a chance to take stock of the new Poland eight years after it cast off communism with cheer-leading from his prestigious pulpit at the Vatican.
"I have seen the changes taking place in my homeland. I have admired the enterprise of my countrymen, their initiative and willingness to work for the good of the country," he said.
Poland's economy is one of the fastest growing in the former Soviet bloc, and the country is on the fast-track to join Western structures such as NATO and the European Union.
The Pope, in his farewell address, appeared to back these aspirations, saying Poland was ready "to offer its own creative contribution to the common treasure of the great family of European nations."

But during the trip that took him from cosmopolitan Krakow with its opera and old town to peasant countryside of rolling fields, dotted with humps of hay, he expressed concern over how his countrymen were using their new wealth and liberties.
"Obviously, there are also many problems needing to be solved," he said.
"I am convinced Poles will find in themselves the wisdom and perseverance necessary for building a just Poland which can guarantee a worthy life for all its citizens," the Pope said.

President Aleksander Kwasniewski, an ex-communist, thanked the Pope for words that would help Poles overcome weaknesses, avoid inflaming hatreds and "find the ability for cooperation among all -- left, the right and the centre."
"These have been great days," Kwasniewski said in an address at the airport, inviting the Pope to return.
The Pope, saying he hoped that his trip would "serve the Church in Poland, my country and all my fellow countrymen," urged Poles to remain faithful to their Christian roots.
During the trip, he told Poles that despite recent social changes, Catholicism was an inextricable part of Poland's national identity and had to remain an influential force.
"My wish for my countrymen, and for Poland, is that she will be able... to be faithful to herself and to the roots from which she has grown," he said at the departure ceremony.
During his journey, the Pope spoke out forcefully several times on what is perhaps the most burning issue dividing the Church and state as well as many Poles -- abortion.
He railed against the practice, saying that otherwise successful societies were still barbarian if they allowed it.

Whether abortion should remain liberalised or be restricted has become a key issue in the campaign for elections due in September, in which a powerful alliance around the pro-Catholic Solidarity union is challenging the ruling ex-communists.
